Plates move because of three driving forces: mantle convection (slow churning of hot rock), slab pull (a sinking plate edge pulling the rest), and ridge push (raised ridges pushing plates apart). Imagine a drone racing course: each drone's path depends on pushes and pulls along the track, like plates depend on these forces.
Relative motion between plates is measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹). That is slow, like fingernail growth, but it adds up over millions of years.

Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? First, stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Think of it like a drone held against a wall by wind: the strain grows until it suddenly breaks free.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries

Why do earthquakes cluster at boundaries? First, stress accumulation: plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Think of it like a drone motor held at full power while the frame is clamped; the stored force releases all at once when the clamp slips.
Three more reasons focus earthquakes at the edges. Fault geometry: pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Rheological contrast: cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, so deformation focuses in the brittle part. Geometric incompatibility: curved plate margins force localized shear zones.

## Plate Speeds and the Ring of Fire
Plates move at set speeds. The Pacific Plate moves northwest at about 5 cm per year. The Nazca Plate slides under South America at about 8 cm per year.
These speeds explain why big earthquakes happen so often along the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire'. Think of it like a drone race: the faster a drone flies, the more often it hits a gate. Faster plates store and release strain more often.
Earthquake depth also follows a pattern. Shallow events (10 km or less) dominate ridges and transform faults. Deeper events (30–300 km) happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone of a subducting slab.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has steps: 1. Interseismic — the locked zone stores strain (decades to centuries) 2. Coseismic — sudden slip releases the energy (seconds to minutes) 3. Postseismic — afterslip and relaxation move stress around (months to years) 4. Preseismic — possible warning signals, like foreshocks or slow slip
Think of it like a chess opening: the long interseismic phase is the slow build-up of position, and the coseismic slip is the sudden attack that releases all the stored tension at once.
For hazard work, seismic gap theory says: a segment that has not ruptured in a full cycle is a candidate for a future large event. GPS and InSAR measure plate speeds in cm per year to refine coupling models.
Common wrong idea: a gap that has been quiet for a long time is safe. It is the opposite — the stored strain makes it a candidate for a large event. Restated once more: no recent rupture means stored energy, not safety.

Think of it like a drone racing course: the low gates (shallow quakes) sit along the ridge and transform tracks, while the deep gates only appear where one plate dives under another. The depth pattern tells you which course you are on.
Depth matters for hazard. The depth distribution of seismicity informs the likely rupture extent and tsunami potential. A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.

## Seismic Gap Theory and Hazard Assessment
Seismic gap theory says a fault segment that has not ruptured during a full seismic cycle is a candidate for a future large earthquake. Think of it like a chess opening you have never played in a long tournament: the move is still available, so it may come soon.
A full seismic cycle has stages: interseismic (strain builds in a locked zone), coseismic (sudden slip releases energy), postseismic (afterslip and relaxation), and possible preseismic signals. A segment that skips the coseismic stage keeps its stored strain.
Hazard assessment uses this idea in a probabilistic way. GPS and InSAR measure plate speeds in cm per year to refine coupling models, showing where strain is still stored.
Restated once more: no recent rupture means stored strain, so that segment is a likely place for the next large event.

These speeds feed into coupling models. A coupling model describes how much a plate boundary is locked and storing strain. Better velocity data means a better model of where strain builds up.

Depth also follows plate setting. Shallow events, at 10 km or less, dominate ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events, 30–300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs. A subduction quake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
